    Chapter 14

    TLS and HTTPS: Putting It All Together

    🤔 In about 100 milliseconds, your browser and a server on another continent run almost everything from Chapters 4 to 13. Let’s watch it happen in slow motion.

    • ⏱️ ~10 min
    • 📚 16 sections
    • 🎮 2 interactive
    • ⭐ 240 XP
    • 🔑 1 fragment

    This is where every building block in the guide comes together.

    14.1What TLS is#

    TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the protocol that protects data traveling between two programs over a network. Its older name was SSL (Secure Sockets Layer), and people still say "SSL certificate" out of habit.

    HTTPS is HTTP (the web) running inside TLS. TLS also protects email (IMAPS, SMTP with STARTTLS), many VPNs, database connections, app APIs, smart-home devices and DNS over TLS/HTTPS.

    What TLS gives you:

    • ✅ Confidentiality: nobody on the path can read the data.
    • ✅ Integrity: nobody can change the data without being detected.
    • ✅ Server authentication: you're talking to the real bank.example, proven by its certificate.
    • ✅ Optional client authentication (mutual TLS).
    • ✅ Forward secrecy (TLS 1.3 always; TLS 1.2 if configured with ECDHE).

    What TLS does NOT give you:

    • ❌ Protection of data once it reaches the server (that's the server's job).
    • ❌ Proof that the website is honest (phishing sites have TLS too).
    • ❌ Hiding which domain you visited (partly fixed by encrypted DNS and ECH).
    • ❌ Protection from malware on your own device.
    ✔ section read

    14.2TLS versions#

    Version Year Status
    SSL 2.0 1995 ❌ Broken
    SSL 3.0 1996 ❌ Broken (POODLE attack, 2014)
    TLS 1.0 1999 ❌ Deprecated (officially in 2021)
    TLS 1.1 2006 ❌ Deprecated (2021)
    TLS 1.2 2008 ⚠️ Still widely used; safe only with modern settings
    TLS 1.3 2018 ✅ Current standard: faster, simpler, safer

    TLS 1.3 removed a large list of old, risky options: RSA key transport (no forward secrecy), CBC-mode ciphers, RC4, SHA-1, MD5, compression and renegotiation. What's left is a small set of choices that are all secure.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    SSL/TLS versions

    ❌ Avoid
    SSL 2.0 / 3.0

    1995 / 1996

    • Started web encryption
    • POODLE, DROWN; fundamentally broken
    Best for: Disable everywhere
    ❌ Avoid
    TLS 1.0 / 1.1

    1999 / 2006

    • Widely compatible in their day
    • BEAST, SHA-1/MD5 internals
    • Deprecated in 2021
    Best for: Disable everywhere
    ⚠️ Legacy
    TLS 1.2

    2008

    • Universal support
    • Secure with ECDHE + AEAD
    • Many dangerous options to misconfigure
    • 2-round-trip handshake
    Best for: Fallback for old clients
    ✅ Use it
    TLS 1.3

    2018

    • 1-RTT handshake; encrypts more of it
    • Only secure options left
    • Forward secrecy always
    • 0-RTT data is replayable
    • Breaks some legacy middleboxes
    Best for: Everything new
    ✔ section read

    14.4The TLS 1.3 handshake, step by step#

    The handshake is a short conversation at the start of the connection in which client and server agree on a key and the server proves its identity. Here it is in full:

    What each step is for, in plain words:

    1. ClientHello: the browser says what it supports and, to save time, guesses the key-exchange method and sends its half of the key exchange right away.
    2. ServerHello: the server picks the options and sends its half of the key exchange.
    3. Shared secret: both sides now compute the same secret, just like Alice and Bob in Chapter 10. Eve, who saw both public halves, can't. HKDF turns it into encryption keys.
    4. EncryptedExtensions: remaining settings, now encrypted (TLS 1.3 encrypts much more of the handshake than TLS 1.2).
    5. Certificate: the server's ID card (Chapter 13).
    6. CertificateVerify: the crucial anti-Mallory step. The server signs the whole conversation with its certificate's private key. Mallory could copy the certificate but can't produce this signature. And because the signature covers the key-exchange values, Mallory can't swap in her own key-exchange values either.
    7. Finished: a MAC over all handshake messages, using the new keys. If anyone altered anything (for example, removing strong cipher suites to force a weaker choice), the MACs won't match and the connection is aborted.
    8. Browser checks everything listed in section 13.5.
    9. Client Finished: the browser confirms its side.
    10. Application data flows, protected by AEAD encryption.

    All of this takes one round trip. If the server doesn't support the key-exchange method the browser guessed, it sends a HelloRetryRequest and the browser tries again, costing an extra round trip.

    Where every chapter of this guide shows up in TLS

    TLS ingredient What it does Chapter
    Random numbers in ClientHello/ServerHello Make every session unique 4
    X25519 / ML-KEM key shares Agree on a shared secret in public, with forward secrecy 10
    HKDF key schedule Derive separate keys for each direction and purpose 8
    Certificate chain Proves the public key belongs to example.com 13
    CertificateVerify (ECDSA, RSA-PSS or Ed25519) Proves the server holds the private key 11
    Transcript hash (SHA-256/384) A fingerprint of the whole handshake 6
    Finished messages (HMAC) Detect any tampering with the handshake 7
    AES-GCM / ChaCha20-Poly1305 Encrypt and authenticate the actual data 5

    14.5TLS 1.2, for comparison#

    You'll still see TLS 1.2 in older systems. Its handshake takes two round trips, and the certificate is sent unencrypted:

    TLS 1.2 also allowed RSA key transport: the client encrypted the secret with the server's RSA key, with no forward secrecy (Chapter 10). A well-configured TLS 1.2 server today only allows ECDHE key exchange with AEAD ciphers.

    ✔ section read

    14.6Cipher suites, decoded#

    A cipher suite is a named combination of algorithms.

    A TLS 1.2 cipher suite names everything:

    A TLS 1.3 cipher suite only names the encryption and hash, because key exchange and signatures are negotiated separately (as "groups" and "signature algorithms"):

    TLS 1.3 defines only five suites:

    TLS 1.3 cipher suite Notes
    TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 ✅ Most common
    TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 ✅ Common
    TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 ✅ Preferred on devices without AES hardware
    TLS_AES_128_CCM_SHA256 IoT devices
    TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256 IoT, shorter tag; not recommended for general use

    Red flags in older cipher suites (avoid any that contain): NULL (no encryption), anon (no authentication), EXPORT (deliberately weakened 1990s crypto), RC4, DES, 3DES, MD5, and TLS_RSA_WITH_... (static RSA key exchange, no forward secrecy).

    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ✔ section read

    14.7After the handshake: the record protocol#

    Once keys are agreed, data is split into records (up to 16 KB each). Each record is encrypted with the AEAD cipher, using a sequence number as part of the nonce. That means:

    • Every record has a unique nonce (no nonce reuse).
    • If an attacker deletes, reorders or replays a record, decryption fails.
    • Long-lived connections can switch to fresh keys with a KeyUpdate message.
    ✔ section read

    14.8Resumption and 0-RTT#

    Reconnecting to a site you visited recently can skip some work. The server gives the client a session ticket (a pre-shared key) at the end of the first connection. Next time, the client presents the ticket and they resume quickly.

    TLS 1.3 even allows 0-RTT ("zero round trip") mode, where the client sends its first request together with the ClientHello. It's fast, but that early data can be replayed by an attacker (sent again to the server). So servers should only accept 0-RTT for harmless, repeatable requests like loading a page, never for "transfer money."

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Session resumption

    ✅ Use it
    Resumption (PSK)

    Reuse a ticket from last time

    • Skips certificate checks: faster
    • Less CPU on busy servers
    • Ticket keys must be rotated or they weaken forward secrecy
    Best for: Returning visitors
    👍 Situational
    0-RTT

    Send data with the first packet

    • Zero waiting on repeat visits
    • Early data can be replayed
    • Only safe for idempotent requests (GETs)
    Best for: Static content
    ✔ section read

    14.9SNI and Encrypted Client Hello (ECH)#

    One server often hosts hundreds of websites on one IP address. To know which certificate to present, it needs to know which site you want before encryption starts. So the ClientHello includes the domain name in a field called SNI (Server Name Indication), unencrypted. Anyone watching can see which site you're visiting, even with HTTPS.

    Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) fixes this. The website publishes a public key in DNS; the browser uses it to encrypt the real ClientHello (including the domain name) inside an outer ClientHello that shows only a generic name, like the hosting provider's. Cloudflare and major browsers support ECH, and it's spreading.

    ✔ section read

    14.10HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC#

    • ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation) is the part of the handshake where client and server agree on HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 or HTTP/3.
    • HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, a newer transport built on UDP. QUIC has TLS 1.3 built in: the transport handshake and the crypto handshake happen together, so a new connection takes one round trip instead of two (TCP + TLS). QUIC also encrypts most of its own packet headers.
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    HTTP versions

    ✅ Use it
    HTTP/2

    Over TLS + TCP

    • Multiplexes many requests on one connection
    • TCP head-of-line blocking on lossy networks
    Best for: Default for most sites
    ✅ Use it
    HTTP/3 (QUIC)

    TLS 1.3 built into QUIC over UDP

    • Faster setup; no head-of-line blocking
    • Survives network changes (Wi-Fi → 4G)
    • UDP sometimes blocked
    • Harder for middleboxes to inspect
    Best for: Mobile and global sites
    ✔ section read

    14.11Mutual TLS (mTLS)#

    In normal TLS, only the server shows a certificate. The client usually proves who it is later, with a password or a cookie. In mutual TLS, both sides present certificates during the handshake.

    mTLS is used for service-to-service traffic inside companies (often managed by "service meshes" such as Istio or Linkerd), "zero trust" networks, IoT devices, banking APIs and VPNs. You tried it in Step 8 of the PKI lab.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Mutual TLS

    ✅ Use it
    mTLS

    Both sides show certificates

    • Strong machine identity, no passwords
    • Zero-trust networks
    • Certificate issuance and rotation for every client
    • Painful for human users
    Best for: Service-to-service traffic
    ✔ section read

    14.12HSTS: closing the HTTP loophole#

    Most people type bank.example, not https://bank.example. The browser's first request may go out over plain HTTP, and the server then redirects to HTTPS. That first unencrypted moment is an opening.

    📜 SSL stripping (2009). Security researcher Moxie Marlinspike released a tool called sslstrip. An attacker on the network intercepts that first HTTP request, talks HTTPS to the bank on the victim's behalf, and keeps talking plain HTTP to the victim. The victim never sees a certificate error, just a missing padlock that most people don't notice.

    The fix is HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security). The server sends a header:

    It tells the browser: "For the next year, only ever connect to me over HTTPS, and don't let the user click through certificate errors." Sites can also join the HSTS preload list, built into browsers, so even the very first visit is protected. Modern browsers additionally offer "HTTPS-First" or "HTTPS-Only" modes.

    ✔ section read

    14.13TLS interception: the "approved" man-in-the-middle#

    Some corporate networks, antivirus products and parental-control tools inspect HTTPS traffic. They work by installing their own root certificate on your device. The proxy then generates a fake certificate for every site on the fly, signed by that root. Your device trusts it, so you see no warning.

    To check whether this is happening, look at the certificate's issuer in your browser. If google.com was issued by "Contoso Corp Security Proxy," your traffic is being inspected. Poorly built interception products have historically weakened security, for example by not checking the real site's certificate properly.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    TLS interception

    ⚠️ Legacy
    Corporate TLS inspection

    An “approved” man in the middle

    • Lets companies scan for malware and data leaks
    • Breaks end-to-end security
    • Middleboxes often validate certificates badly
    • One box sees every secret
    Best for: Only with careful policy
    ✔ section read

    14.14Common certificate errors and what they mean#

    Browser error (Chrome style) Meaning Common cause
    NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID Certificate expired or not yet valid Forgotten renewal, or your computer's clock is wrong
    NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID The name doesn't match the certificate's SAN Wrong certificate installed, or visiting example.com with a certificate for www.example.com only
    NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID The chain doesn't lead to a trusted root Self-signed certificate, private CA, missing intermediate, or interception
    NET::ERR_CERT_REVOKED The certificate was cancelled Key compromise or mis-issuance
    ERR_SSL_VERSION_OR_CIPHER_MISMATCH No common TLS version or cipher A very old server or client
    Warning with no "proceed anyway" link The site uses HSTS You can't (and shouldn't) bypass it

    Explore these safely at badssl.com, which hosts deliberately broken test sites (expired.badssl.com, self-signed.badssl.com, wrong.host.badssl.com …).

    ✔ section read

    14.15Hands-on with TLS#

    🧪 Try it yourself:

    Terminal
    # A quick summary of a site's TLS connection
openssl s_client -connect www.google.com:443 -servername www.google.com -brief </dev/null
# CONNECTION ESTABLISHED
# Protocol version: TLSv1.3
# Ciphersuite: TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
# Peer certificate: CN=www.google.com
# Hash used: SHA256
# Signature type: ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256
# Verification: OK
# Negotiated TLS1.3 group: X25519MLKEM768        ← post-quantum hybrid key exchange!

# Force a specific TLS version (does the server still allow TLS 1.2?)
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -tls1_2 -brief </dev/null

# Check when a site's certificate expires
echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -enddate

    In Python:

    Python
    import socket, ssl

ctx = ssl.create_default_context()      # verifies certificates and hostnames by default
with socket.create_connection(("example.com", 443)) as sock:
    with ctx.wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname="example.com") as tls:
        print(tls.version())            # TLSv1.3
        print(tls.cipher())             # ('TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384', 'TLSv1.3', 256)
        cert = tls.getpeercert()
        print(cert["subject"], cert["issuer"], cert["notAfter"])

    (If Python reports CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED on macOS, run the "Install Certificates.command" script that comes with the python.org installer, or pip install certifi and pass cafile=certifi.where() to create_default_context.)

    ⚠️ Watch out: never "fix" certificate errors in code by turning verification off (verify=False in Python's requests, curl -k, InsecureSkipVerify in Go, rejectUnauthorized: false in Node.js). That silently removes all protection against man-in-the-middle attacks. It's one of the most common security bugs in real software.

    Great free tools for going deeper:

    • SSL Labs Server Test: grades any public website's TLS configuration.
    • The Illustrated TLS 1.3 Connection: every byte of a real handshake, explained.
    • Mozilla SSL Configuration Generator: secure server settings for nginx, Apache and others.
    • Wireshark + SSLKEYLOGFILE: if you start Chrome or Firefox with the environment variable SSLKEYLOGFILE=/path/to/keys.log, the browser writes its session keys to that file, and Wireshark can use it to decrypt your own captured HTTPS traffic. It's a great way to see the handshake messages above for real.
    ✔ section read

    14.16A secure TLS setup checklist (for people running servers)#

    • ✅ Enable TLS 1.3, keep TLS 1.2 only for older clients, and disable everything older.
    • ✅ Allow only ECDHE key exchange and AEAD ciphers (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305).
    • ✅ Use an ECDSA P-256 certificate (or RSA 2048+), and serve the full chain.
    • ✅ Automate certificate renewal with ACME, and monitor expiry anyway.
    • ✅ Send HSTS; consider preloading.
    • ✅ Redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
    • ✅ Set a CAA record and monitor Certificate Transparency logs for your domains.
    • ✅ Keep your TLS library (OpenSSL, BoringSSL, etc.) up to date.
    ✔ section read
